title: Double vs Basis Close Management Review (August 2026)
summary: August 2026 breakdown of Double vs Basis close software. See which tool runs close work in the ledger and which one tracks it from the outside.
body_text: If your team is spending time on the close but not saving time on it, the tool you're using might be tracking work without doing it. Basis and Double both show up in searches for accounting firm close software, but they take fundamentally different approaches. Here's where they split. TLDR: Basis handles task coordination and client communication, but reconciliations, journal entries, and variance analysis still happen outside the tool. The core architectural difference: Basis informs the workflow with AI suggestions; Double's AI posts results directly to the ledger. Double's per-client pricing starts at $10 monthly with no user fees, scaling in proportion to revenue as your firm grows. Firms using Double report saving 30 to 50 percent of close time per engagement by automating data prep, not by cutting corners on the work. Double executes close work across reconciliations, flux analysis, accruals, and client communication in one system, starting at $10 per client monthly. What Is Basis? Basis is a close management software for accounting firms built for accounting firms. It sits in the same general category as Double, targeting firms that run recurring month-end close work across multiple clients. The product is built around task management and workflow coordination. Firms use it to assign close steps to team members, track progress across client engagements, and keep recurring checklists organized. The interface is built around a list-based view of tasks, with statuses that move from open to in-progress to complete as work gets done. Basis also includes a client-facing portal where firms can request documents, share deliverables, and communicate with clients without bouncing between email threads. That portal sits alongside the task management layer, separate from the close workflow itself. Where Basis Focuses The design philosophy behind Basis leans toward coordination and visibility. It gives firm owners a cleaner view of where each client engagement stands, which is a real improvement over spreadsheet-based tracking or generic project tools. The task and month-end close checklist system lets firms build recurring close templates that auto-populate each month, reducing the setup time for repeat engagements. Client communication lives inside the tool, so document requests and approvals have a paper trail separate from email. Progress tracking gives managers a high-level view of which clients are on schedule and which are falling behind. Basis runs AI agents that execute accounting workflows and deliver finished output for review. The distinction worth understanding is where that output lands: Basis surfaces completed work into a review queue for an accountant to approve, so the results sit above the ledger until someone acts on them. Double posts results directly to the ledger through two-way sync, so reconciliations, journal entries, and variance explanations flow into the books without a separate approval-and-export step. What Is Double? Double is close management software built for accounting firms running multi-client workflows. Where most close tools were designed for a single internal finance team, Double was built from the ground up to handle the parallel complexity of managing multiple client closes simultaneously, each with its own ledger, checklist, and deadline. The core idea is execution over tracking. Double connects directly to QuickBooks Online and Xero via two-way sync, so changes flow in both directions without manual exports or copy-paste handoffs. From there, AI handles the repetitive data work: matching transactions, drafting variance explanations, flagging anomalies, and preparing journal entries for review. What Double Actually Does Firms using Double report saving 30 to 50 percent of close time per engagement, in an industry where industry estimates suggest automation can reduce close time by 25 to 40 percent or more. The product covers: AI-powered transaction matching that categorizes and matches transactions against the live ledger, so accountants review decisions instead of making them from scratch. Flux analysis that automatically drafts variance explanations at the vendor and transaction level across the P&L and Balance Sheet, with configurable materiality thresholds. Accruals and prepaids management that handles prepaid expense amortization, fixed asset depreciation, deferred revenue, and loan amortization schedules directly inside the close workflow. A client-facing portal for document requests, approvals, and communication, keeping everything tied to the close instead of scattered across email threads. Multi-client portfolio views so firm staff can see close status, bottlenecks, and outstanding items across every active engagement in one place. Pricing follows a per-client model with no user fees or software charges, which keeps costs tied to the work being done, not headcount. AI Execution: Where Output Actually Lands AI tools are only as useful as the work they actually complete. The distinction worth understanding here is where each tool's output lands after the AI runs. Basis Close's AI surfaces suggestions, drafts explanations, and flags anomalies. The output typically lands in a review queue where an accountant then decides what to do next. That review step is often appropriate, but it means the AI is informing the workflow without executing inside it. Double's AI posts directly to the ledger. When the flux analysis runs, it drafts variance explanations at the vendor and transaction level across the P&L and Balance Sheet, with configurable materiality thresholds so teams can control depth and scope. When accruals run, Double calculates recognition amounts, prepares journal entries, and posts them automatically. The accountant starts from conclusions, not raw inputs. There are three specific output behaviors that separate the two approaches: Flux analysis in Double auto-drafts variance explanations with configurable materiality thresholds, so controllers review finished narratives instead of rebuilding variance stories from scratch. Accrual and prepaid management handles prepaid expense amortization, fixed asset depreciation, deferred revenue, and loan amortization schedules inside the close workflow, not in a separate spreadsheet handed off after the fact. Journal entries post directly through two-way sync with QuickBooks Online and Xero for accounting firms, and Sage Intacct and NetSuite for corporate finance teams, so the ledger reflects close work in real time. The structural difference is that Double's AI is wired into the execution layer. Basis Close treats AI as a decision-support layer sitting above the workflow. For teams where the bottleneck is review volume, that distinction changes how much close time actually comes back. Dimension Double Basis Where AI output lands Posts directly to the ledger through two-way sync Surfaces into a review queue for accountant approval Close execution Reconciliations, flux analysis, accruals, and journal entries run inside the workflow Agents execute work and deliver finished output for review Ledger integration Two-way sync with QuickBooks Online and Xero for firms; Sage Intacct and NetSuite for corporate finance Task and workflow coordination sits above the ledger Client communication Client portal built into the close workflow, tied to the tasks it unblocks Client portal alongside the task management layer Pricing model Per connected client at $10, $25, or $50 monthly, no user fees Per-user model with annual commitments Time to value Live within days; hands-on three-month implementation included for contracts over ten clients Broader workflow scope tends to extend onboarding timelines Close Management and Practice-Wide Workflow Basis positions itself as a close management tool built for corporate accounting teams. The workflow is organized around task assignment, preparer/reviewer sign-offs, and status tracking across a structured checklist. Teams can attach workpapers, leave comments, and move items through approval stages without leaving the tool. For a single-entity internal finance team running a predictable close cadence, that architecture holds up reasonably well. The friction appears when the close requires more than coordination. Where Basis Stops Short Basis runs AI agents that execute accounting workflows and deliver finished output for review. What it does not do is post that output directly to the ledger. Reconciliations, flux analysis, accruals, and journal entries surface into a review queue, where an accountant approves the work before it lands in the books. That distinction matters because in most month-end close processes , the volume of review-and-approve steps is where time piles up. Every result that lands in a queue for sign-off before it reaches the books adds a handoff. Double takes a different approach. Instead of sitting on top of the close as a coordination layer, Double runs the work directly inside the workflow: Reconciliations auto-populate from two-way sync with QuickBooks Online, Xero, Sage Intacct, or NetSuite, so preparers match transactions against live ledger data without toggling between systems. AI flux analysis drafts variance explanations at the vendor and transaction level across the P&L and Balance Sheet, with configurable materiality thresholds. Reviewers start from conclusions, not raw inputs to reconstruct. Month-end close automation handles accruals, prepaids, depreciation schedules, and deferred revenue entries calculated and posted automatically inside the close workflow. Journal entries are prepared and submitted directly to the GL through the same two-way sync, with no export step. The structural difference is where the output lands. Basis surfaces finished work into a review queue that sits above the ledger until someone approves it. Double posts results straight to the ledger through two-way sync, so the books reflect the close as the work completes. Client Communication and the Document Collection Layer Both tools handle client communication, but they take structurally different approaches to how document collection fits into the close workflow. Firms comparing financial close management software will find these distinctions matter at scale. Basis treats client communication as a core product feature. Its client portal lets firms send document requests, collect responses, and track outstanding items in one place. Clients receive a branded experience without needing to log into the accounting software itself. For firms where the bottleneck is chasing clients for bank statements, receipts, and supporting schedules, this is a real workflow advantage. Double's client portal covers the same territory. Firms can send document requests directly from inside the close workflow, and clients respond through a clean, purpose-built interface. The key structural difference is that in Double, document collection and close execution sit in the same system. When a client uploads a bank statement, the reconciliation it feeds is right there. There is no handoff between a communication layer and a close layer, because they are the same layer. Why the Separation Matters When document collection lives in a separate tool from the actual close work, gaps open in the seams. A request gets marked complete in one system while the underlying task in the close checklist stays open. Someone has to manually bridge that gap. Double removes that bridging step by connecting client responses directly to the close tasks they unblock, which matters most when teams want to automate the financial close end to end. Pricing and Time-to-Value Pricing structures reveal a lot about how a software company thinks about its customers. With Double and Basis, the gap is structural, not merely numerical. Double charges per connected client, starting at $10 per client monthly, with no user fees and no software charges layered on top. Accounting firms pay for the clients they actively manage, which means the cost scales in direct proportion to revenue. There are no seat licenses to negotiate and no surprise charges as the team grows. Basis pricing is less transparent. Published information points to a per-user pricing model with annual commitments, which creates a different kind of cost math and a structural disadvantage compared to purpose-built bookkeeping practice management software that aligns cost with client volume. As firms add staff or bring on new clients, the seat count climbs independently of revenue, and the annual lock-in reduces flexibility during periods of growth or contraction. Time-to-value follows a similar pattern. Double connects to QuickBooks Online and Xero through two-way sync, and firms report being live within days, not weeks. For contracts over ten clients, hands-on three-month implementation is included in the price. Basis targets a broader workflow scope, which tends to extend onboarding timelines. The more a tool tries to do, the longer it takes before it feels settled. Basis Close is a capable tool for accounting firms that want structured close workflows with built-in client communication. If your firm runs light client volumes, values a clean interface, and needs a straightforward checklist experience, Basis fills that role reasonably well, though firms comparing similar tools may also find the Double vs Karbon comparison useful for assessing practice management fit. The fit breaks down when close complexity scales. Basis handles task coordination and client requests, but the actual accounting work (variance analysis, accrual entries, prepaid amortization, transaction matching) still lives outside the tool. Your team finishes tasks in Basis and does the analysis elsewhere, which means the close is tracked but never fully executed in one place. Double is built for firms where that gap creates real friction. Who Gets the Most From Double Three firm profiles tend to see the strongest results: Firms running five or more concurrent client closes, where toggling between a task tracker and a spreadsheet creates compounding delays across the portfolio, not a single isolated slowdown. Firms where controllers and senior staff spend meaningful time on manual data work like pulling trial balance exports, rebuilding variance narratives, and formatting workpapers, which AI can take off their plate so they focus on review and judgment. Firms where client communication, task ownership, and accounting execution all need to live in one audit trail, not spread across three separate tools. Firms using Double report saving 30 to 50 percent of close time per engagement. That figure comes from automating the data prep that precedes real accounting work, not from cutting corners on the work itself. If your firm is at that inflection point where growth is straining your current close process, the architecture difference between the two tools matters more than any individual feature comparison. Final Thoughts on Double vs Basis for Close Management Basis and Double are not competing for the same use case. Double runs the close end to end; Basis coordinates the workflow around it. For firms where the real cost is in manual data work and toggling between systems, the architecture difference between the two tools changes what your team gets back every month. See how Double works in practice before your next close cycle.

title: 10 Best Explainer Video Companies in USA for 2026
summary: We verified every US address. See the 10 best explainer video companies in USA, what they charge, and which studios are not American at all.
body_text: Key takeaways: Several studios ranking for "explainer video companies in USA" are not in the USA. Five candidates we checked publish addresses in Toronto, Bangalore or Sydney, and two of them rank on page one for the American keyword. The largest study of video engagement ever run, covering 6.9 million viewing sessions, found that shorter videos are much more engaging. Length is the cheapest lever you have. Federal wage data puts a staff animator's median pay at $99,800 a year before benefits, with the occupation growing only 2 percent, so most teams commission explainers rather than hire for them. Ask any studio for a street address before you ask for a quote. It is the fastest way to filter a shortlist, and almost nobody does it. An explainer video is the format you reach for when your product cannot be photographed and will not be read about. Software, financial products, medical devices, anything that happens inside a server or a sealed tank: a camera is useless and a landing page full of text goes unread. The problem is that "explainer video company in USA" is one of the least trustworthy queries in this category. The phrase appears in the page titles of studios based in Ontario and Karnataka, and the roundups ranking for it repeat those studios without checking. We went looking for American animation studios and spent most of the research time disqualifying candidates. What follows is the list that survived. We put ourselves at the top and then spent the rest of this piece marking out which briefs belong with a specialist studio instead. On a character-led film or a broadcast campaign, one of the nine below is the better call. Treat the video as a working asset rather than a one-off expense, an argument we make at length about design for advertising , because the studios that price well on a single film often price badly on the variants you will need six months later. What counts as an explainer video company The category is broader than it looks, and picking the wrong kind of supplier is the most common reason a project runs to double the estimate. A dedicated explainer studio makes narrated 2D animation, 60 to 120 seconds, aimed at making an abstract product legible. That is the core product. Around it sit whiteboard and scribe animation, which trades polish for a sense of being walked through something; product demo animation built from real interface recordings; character animation, where the story carries more weight than the feature list; and motion graphics for social cutdowns. Each has a different cost base. A whiteboard video and a character-driven brand film share almost no production steps, which is why a brief that just says "animated explainer" invites wildly different quotes from equally honest studios. Decide which of those five formats applies, settle the runtime, and name the channel it plays on, all before you contact anyone. A clear brief is worth more than a longer shortlist, and it is the part most buyers skip. Our own creative brief guide walks through the questions a studio will otherwise have to guess at. How we verified this list, and what it disqualified Every competing roundup on this keyword republishes directory rankings without opening the sites. We did the opposite: we resolved each candidate's real domain by search, loaded it, and read the company's own contact or about page for a street address. That single check removed more candidates than any quality judgment did. Hatch Studios is in Toronto. Its own about page describes its founder as one of Canada's leading animation creative directors, and its client list includes The Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada. It ranks on page one for the American keyword. MotionGility publishes a Canadian address on Ellesmere Road in Scarborough, Ontario, while its page title reads "Best Explainer Video Company in USA." Epic Video Factory lists Dundas Street West in Toronto. Studiotale titles its homepage "Animated Explainer Videos Company in Bangalore, India." Punchy Studio , which appears in US-facing explainer searches, runs on a .com.au domain and calls itself Australia's leading visual communications agency. Three more candidates failed for different reasons. Grumo Media publishes no location anywhere on its homepage, about page or contact page, so we could not confirm it either way and dropped it rather than guess. The Draw Shop now runs under the banner "Powered by Explainify," meaning it is no longer an independent choice. Explainly blocks automated access from three separate directions, so we could not verify its pages the way we verified everyone else's. Most lists of the top explainer video companies in USA never run this check at all. None of this makes those studios bad, and several are excellent, so a Toronto animator may well be the right hire. But an article promising American companies should contain American companies, and a buyer who needs a US entity for procurement, contracting or time-zone reasons deserves to know before the first call. The list runs to ten rather than the usual twelve because padding it would have meant putting a Toronto studio in a USA roundup. The 10 best explainer video companies in USA The table sorts by what each company is actually built to make, which predicts fit better than a star rating. Just one company on this list posts rates publicly, so treat the pricing column as a tier indicator rather than a quote. Company Based in Best for What it makes Pricing Awesomic San Francisco, CA Explainers plus the design around them Animation, motion, web, brand, video $1,490 or $2,995 monthly Sharp Eye Animation San Francisco, CA Custom animation with a tech sensibility 2D and 3D animated explainers Quote only Digital Brew Orlando, FL Full-service animated explainer projects 2D, 3D and live-action hybrid Quote only TruScribe Madison, WI Whiteboard explanation of complex ideas Scribe and whiteboard animation Quote only Next Day Animations Baltimore, MD and Minneapolis, MN Mission-driven and nonprofit work 2D explainers, illustration, voiceover Quote only IdeaRocket Miami, FL Corporate animation with a long catalog 2D, 3D, whiteboard, motion graphics Quote only Nathan Love New York, NY Character animation with awards behind it Character-led animation and design Quote only Trollbäck+Company New York, NY Brand films rather than feature tours Brand identity in motion Quote only Killer Visual Strategies Seattle, WA Data-heavy stories that need visualizing Motion, infographics, interactive Quote only Big Fish Presentations Baton Rouge, LA Explainers that live inside a pitch Presentation design and video Quote only Locations in that table come from each company's own site, not from a directory listing. Where a firm publishes more than one office, we named the ones it calls headquarters. 1. Awesomic Best for: teams that need an explainer and then keep needing creative work. We're a design and creative subscription based in San Francisco. You describe the task, the app routes it to a pre-screened animator or designer the same day, and revisions carry no cap. Animation and motion sit alongside web, brand and product design on the same subscription, with a project manager on the dedicated tier. The reason we lead this list is not that we out-animate a specialist character studio. It is that an explainer is almost never the only thing a company needs. The video ships and then the landing page it points at needs rebuilding, the social cutdowns need cutting, and the pitch deck needs to match. Denario is the clearest example we can point to. The fintech company, later acquired by PandaDoc, came to us for animation to simplify how it explained its product. We built a product demo video from a script they had already written, then a full illustration set that became their visual language, social ads for three platforms, a one-pager aimed at restaurants as a new audience, and a multi-language Webflow migration. That is roughly a year of work that began as one video. What we make: animated explainers and product demos, motion graphics and social cutdowns, illustration systems, landing pages and full sites, brand identity, pitch decks. Pricing: two plans cover most animation needs. Graphic Pack runs $1,490 monthly, falling to $1,190 if you commit quarterly against a three-month floor. All-in-One, which folds in no-code build, copywriting and QA, costs $2,995 monthly or $2,396 on that same quarterly basis. Above them sits Dedicated Talent, scoped case by case; below them, AI Designer at $200 for self-serve landing pages. Proof: 20,000-plus completed projects, a client base north of 4,000 companies, 4.9 ratings on Google Play and on Trustpilot, an acceptance rate of 0.82 percent among applying designers, plus Y Combinator backing and a Red Dot Award. Where we fit: we are the right call when the explainer is the first of many things, and the wrong call when you want one broadcast-grade character film and nothing else. For that, hire a specialist below. Our case studies show which of the two situations you are in. Get started 2. Sharp Eye Animation Best for: technology companies that want animation with a product sensibility. Sharp Eye describes itself on its about page as a full-service animated video production company founded by an ex-Googler, headquartered in San Francisco with a presence in Los Angeles. That origin shows in the work, which leans toward software and platform explanation rather than consumer storytelling. It handles the full arc from script through storyboard to final animation, which suits teams that do not have a copywriter ready to hand the studio a finished script. What it makes: 2D animated explainers, 3D animation, product videos, motion graphics. Pricing: no published rate card. Projects are scoped individually. Why buyers shortlist it: a genuine San Francisco address and a founder from a large technology company are an unusual combination in this category, where most studios are either coastal boutiques or offshore production shops. 3. Digital Brew Best for: companies that want one team to own the whole video, end to end. Digital Brew works out of North Magnolia Avenue in Orlando and positions itself squarely as an animated explainer video production company rather than a general creative agency. It is one of the few firms on this list whose entire homepage is about a single deliverable. The studio blends animation with live action on the same project, which is useful when part of your story genuinely can be filmed and part of it cannot. What it makes: 2D and 3D animated explainers, live-action hybrid video, motion graphics, character animation. Pricing: quoted per project, with no public tiers. Its real strength: focus. A studio that does one thing tends to have a repeatable process for it, and Digital Brew's positioning leaves little doubt about what you are buying. 4. TruScribe Best for: dense or technical material that needs to feel like a walkthrough. TruScribe publishes its headquarters address on Seminole Centre Court in Madison, Wisconsin, and has built its practice around whiteboard animation specifically. The company frames the format as a method rather than a style, arguing that watching a hand draw an idea holds attention differently than watching a finished graphic appear. That makes it a narrow pick, but a strong one when the subject is genuinely complicated. What it makes: whiteboard and scribe animation, script development, voiceover, animated training content. Pricing: scoped per project; the site discusses cost ranges in its blog rather than publishing tiers. Where it fits: internal training, compliance, healthcare and any subject where the audience needs to follow a chain of reasoning rather than admire a product. 5. Next Day Animations Best for: nonprofits, agencies and mission-driven organizations on real budgets. Next Day Animations describes its team as animators, voiceover actors and illustrators located across the United States, with offices in Baltimore and Minneapolis. It is the most explicitly distributed company on this list, and it says so plainly rather than implying a single glass headquarters. Much of its published work is for advocacy groups, public agencies and educational organizations, which is a different discipline from product marketing. What it makes: 2D animated explainers, illustration, scriptwriting, voiceover, translation and localization. Why it made this list: it serves a segment that most explainer studios quietly price out, and it does so without pretending to be something it is not. 6. IdeaRocket Best for: corporate buyers who want a deep back catalog to judge from. IdeaRocket has been making animated business video for a long time and has an unusually large public portfolio spanning 2D, 3D, whiteboard and motion graphics. If you want to watch twenty examples before a call, this is the easiest site on the list to do that on. One point of accuracy matters here. IdeaRocket markets itself heavily around New York, but the only postal address it publishes is a private mailbox on Northeast 191st Street in Miami, Florida. We are noting what the site says rather than characterizing where the team sits. What it makes: 2D and 3D animation, whiteboard video, motion graphics, live-action hybrid. Pricing: no public rate card, though the site discusses typical animation cost ranges openly. Why buyers shortlist it: breadth of catalog and a willingness to talk about money before you are on a sales call. 7. Nathan Love Best for: brands that want character animation with genuine craft behind it. Nathan Love is a New York animation studio whose work sits closer to entertainment than to software explanation. Its about page lists recognition including a Shorty Awards win with silver and audience honors, finalist and merit placements at The One Show, a London International Awards shortlist and a bronze at The Global Awards. This is not the studio for a fifteen-slide feature tour. It is the studio for a character your audience remembers. What it makes: character animation, design and art direction, broadcast and social campaigns. Pricing: quoted per project, at the higher end of this list. Where it beats the alternatives: when the brief is emotional rather than instructional, craft stops being a luxury and becomes the entire point. 8. Trollbäck+Company Best for: organizations translating a brand into motion, not explaining a feature. Trollbäck+Company publishes a New York headquarters alongside an annex, plus Stockholm and Los Angeles presence. Its practice is brand identity expressed through motion, and its public work skews toward large institutions and media brands. Include it on a shortlist only if what you actually need is a brand film. Briefing a firm like this on a product walkthrough wastes both parties' time. What it makes: motion-led brand identity, brand films, title design, design systems for video. Pricing: enterprise scoping, no public figures. Its real strength: it treats motion as part of an identity system rather than as a one-off asset, which matters if the video has to sit next to a rebrand. 9. Killer Visual Strategies Best for: research, data and reports that need to become watchable. Formerly Killer Infographics, the Seattle firm now leads with visual communication and describes itself in content marketing terms. Its portfolio is heavy on data visualization, interactive pieces and motion built from research, including regional work such as a Puget Sound technology visualization for the Washington Technology Industry Association. Treat it as an adjacent option rather than a pure explainer shop. If your raw material is a study or a dataset, that adjacency is exactly what you want. What it makes: motion graphics, infographics, interactive experiences, presentation and report design. Pricing: project-based, no public tiers. Why it earns a place here: most explainer studios start from a script. This one starts from evidence, which is a meaningfully different process. 10. Big Fish Presentations Best for: explainers that need to live inside a pitch or a keynote. Big Fish Presentations works from South 14th Street in Baton Rouge and operates alongside ThreeSixtyEight, sharing contact details with it. Its distinctive angle is that video and presentation design are one practice, not two. That is genuinely useful if the video's real job is to open a sales meeting or an investor pitch rather than to sit on a homepage. What it makes: presentation design, animated and live-action video, event content. Pricing: scoped per engagement. Where it fits: fundraising decks, conference keynotes and sales enablement, where the animation has to match the slides that follow it. What an explainer video costs in the US Public rate cards are vanishingly rare here, which makes budgeting harder than it should be. The ranges below reflect what these studios describe in their own public writing about cost, and they move with length, animation style and how much script work you hand over. Style Typical range What drives the number Whiteboard or scribe, 60 to 90 seconds $3,000 to $10,000 Illustration volume and script length Standard 2D animated explainer, 60 to 90 seconds $8,000 to $25,000 Custom illustration versus library assets Character-driven 2D with original design $25,000 to $75,000 Character design, rigging, animation hours 3D or technical animation $30,000 to $150,000 Modeling and render time Ongoing animation on a subscription $1,490 to $2,995 a month Volume and how much non-video work is included Two things move these numbers more than anything else. The first is whether you arrive with a finished script, because script development is often a third of the timeline. The second is revision policy, since a fixed-bid project with two included rounds and a studio charging for the third is a very different commitment from unlimited revisions. It is worth comparing that against building the capability internally. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the 2024 median pay for special effects artists and animators at $99,800 a year, before benefits, software or management overhead, with the occupation projected to grow just 2 percent through 2034 and around 5,000 openings a year. For most companies producing a handful of videos annually, that math does not work, which is why commissioning remains the norm. Recruiting is the other cost nobody budgets, since motion specialists are a thin market and the search itself takes months, a process we break down in our guide to hiring motion design talent . How to choose between them Start with the format, not the vendor. Once you know whether you need a whiteboard walkthrough or a character film, half the list disqualifies itself. Then apply four filters in order: Ask for a street address and confirm it on the company's own site before the first call. Watch three finished videos in your format, not a showreel of best moments from twenty projects. Ask who writes the script, and what happens to the timeline if you supply your own. Get the revision policy in writing, including what a round is and what triggers a new charge. On length, there is better evidence than the usual unsourced claims about attention spans. Guo, Kim and Rubin analyzed 6.9 million video-watching sessions across four edX courses and found that shorter videos are substantially more engaging, and that informal, direct delivery outperformed polished studio production. The finding comes from educational video, but the mechanism is the same one your explainer depends on. The practical read is to cut before you polish. A tight 70-second video from a mid-tier studio will usually outperform a beautiful 3-minute one, and it costs less to make. Deciding between commissioning this and building an in-house function is the same calculation covered in our comparison of creative service models . Making the shortlist call Three questions settle most of these decisions faster than a procurement process will. Is this one video or the first of several? A single flagship film belongs with a specialist studio. A steady stream of product videos, cutdowns and the design that surrounds them belongs on a retainer or a subscription, because per-project pricing punishes volume. Does the story need craft or clarity? Nathan Love and Trollbäck sit at the craft end, TruScribe and Next Day Animations at the clarity end, and most of the list in between. Buying craft when you needed clarity is the most expensive mistake in this category. And does it actually need to be American? If procurement, contracting or security review requires a US entity, the verification above matters a great deal. If it does not, you have a much wider field, and some of the studios we disqualified for location are genuinely strong. Once the video exists, the harder question is usually distribution, which is where planning the surrounding video edit and cutdowns pays for itself. If you want animation to sit alongside the web, brand and social work it inevitably creates, that is what our video service is built for. FAQs How much does an explainer video cost in the USA? Most American studios quote between $8,000 and $25,000 for a standard 60 to 90-second 2D animated explainer. Whiteboard animation runs lower, often $3,000 to $10,000, while character-driven or 3D work starts around $25,000 and climbs past $100,000 for technical animation. The two biggest variables are whether you supply a finished script and how many revision rounds are included. Subscription models price differently, charging monthly rather than per project, which changes the math once you need more than two videos a year. How do I check that an explainer video company is really based in the USA? Open the company's own contact or about page and look for a street address, not a phone number or a "serving clients nationwide" line. Directory listings and roundups routinely describe firms as American when their own sites publish addresses in Toronto, Bangalore or Sydney. If a company publishes no address at all, treat that as a missing answer rather than a neutral one. This single check disqualified five candidates while we were building this list. How long should an explainer video be? Between 60 and 90 seconds for most marketing uses. Research by Guo, Kim and Rubin covering 6.9 million viewing sessions found shorter videos substantially more engaging, and that holds across formats. If your script will not fit, the usual cause is trying to cover several audiences in one video rather than genuinely needing the time. Two short videos aimed at two audiences almost always outperform one long video aimed at both. Should I hire an animation studio or use a design subscription? Hire a studio when you need one flagship piece with a distinctive visual signature, particularly character animation or a brand film. Choose a subscription when animation is one of several ongoing needs and you also require landing pages, social cutdowns, decks and brand assets. The deciding factor is volume rather than quality: per-project pricing works against you as soon as the second and third videos appear, while a monthly model works against you if you genuinely only ever need one. Who writes the script for an explainer video? It varies by studio, and it is worth asking early because script development often accounts for a third of the schedule. Some companies include scriptwriting and treat it as the core of the engagement. Others expect a finished script and will quote a shorter timeline if you have one. Denario handed us a script it had already written and we produced the video from it, which compressed the project considerably. If you have strong internal writers, say so during scoping, because it should change both the price and the delivery date.

title: How Security Reviews Shape Marketplace Deals
summary: Where security review enters a cloud marketplace deal: what the provider checks continuously, what the buyer still asks, and how to shorten both.
body_text: A marketplace deal passes through two security reviews that have nothing to do with each other. The provider checks the artifact, continuously and without asking. The buyer checks the vendor, and no marketplace listing exempts you from it. Teams that plan for one and are surprised by the other lose weeks in the middle of a closing quarter. There is a comfortable assumption that being on AWS Marketplace or Microsoft Marketplace means a security review has already happened, so the buyer’s will be lighter. Half of that is true. A review has happened, and it was rigorous. But it examined a different thing, for a different party, against different criteria — and the buyer’s security team, who did not commission it, will not treat it as evidence of much. Knowing which review is asking what is the difference between answering a questionnaire in two days and answering it in five weeks. The two reviews, side by side The provider reviews your artifact. The buyer reviews your company. Provider certification Buyer security review Who runs it AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud Your customer’s security team What it examines The image, package or SaaS integration Your company’s controls and practices When At submission, then continuously During the deal, sometimes after Evidence it wants A conforming artifact SOC 2, pen test results, questionnaires Consequence of failing Listing hidden or unavailable to new subscribers The deal stops Neither substitutes for the other. Both can stop revenue. What the provider actually checks — and keeps checking The part sellers underestimate is that certification is not an event. AWS states that it “continuously scans products to verify that existing listings continue to meet any changes to these requirements,” and that when a product falls out of compliance, AWS contacts the seller, and “in some cases, products might be temporarily made unavailable to new subscribers until issues are resolved.” Microsoft is blunter still for container offers: “Microsoft performs regular security validations on container offers. If vulnerabilities are identified in a published offer, Microsoft reserves the right to hide/deprecate the offer (with or without advanced notification to the publisher) to ensure the safety of our customers.” So a listing that passed in March can be pulled in September because a dependency aged out, and the first you hear of it may be a customer asking why your product is not there. The AWS bar for machine images is specific and worth checking against your build: “AMIs must pass all security checks and must not contain critical or high-severity unpatched vulnerabilities or malware identified during scanning.” “AMIs must use currently supported operating systems and software. Operating systems and software that reached their end of life are not allowed.” “AMIs must not be older than two years from their creation date.” No hardcoded secrets — “system user and service passwords (including hashed passwords), private keys, or credentials.” No password-based authentication for instance services, and for SSH specifically, PasswordAuthentication set to no with no authorized public keys baked in. “A seller must not have access to instances run by a customer” unless the customer explicitly enables it. The two-year age limit and the end-of-life rule are the ones that catch stable products. A component that has not changed does not need a new version — until the base image ages past the threshold, and then it does. Put a calendar reminder against it, because nothing in your own pipeline will. Microsoft’s general policies add an obligation most sellers never read: under policy 100.11 you “must report suspected security events, including security incidents and vulnerabilities of your Marketplace software and service offerings, at the earliest opportunity.” That is a disclosure duty to Microsoft, separate from anything in your customer contracts. What the buyer asks, and why the marketplace does not help The buyer’s review is about your company. Their questionnaire wants your SOC 2 report, your penetration test summary, your subprocessor list, your data residency, your incident response commitments, your breach notification window. None of this is what the marketplace certified, so “we are on AWS Marketplace” is not an answer to any of it. What the marketplace does change is the shape of the surrounding process: Vendor onboarding is already done. The buyer has a commercial relationship with the cloud provider, so the finance, tax and supplier-registration parts are skipped. The security review is not part of that. The contract may not be yours. If the deal uses standardised terms rather than your own paper, the security commitments in it are the marketplace’s standard ones. If your customer needs specific breach notification timelines or audit rights, those belong in custom terms — EULAs and custom terms in marketplace deals covers which document governs. Nobody schedules it. In a direct deal, procurement triggers security review at a known step. In a marketplace deal, the commercial terms are often agreed first, and the security review arrives late — occasionally after the offer has been sent, occasionally after it has expired. That last point is the practical one. When you need a signature on legal documents in a marketplace deal covers the parallel question for legal, and the answer is the same in both cases: the step did not disappear, it just lost its place in the sequence. Shortening both Publish the answers before you are asked. A security page carrying your certifications, subprocessors and architecture summary answers most of a questionnaire without a call. Suger publishes its own for exactly this reason. Keep an evidence pack current. SOC 2 report, most recent penetration test summary, architecture diagram, data flow description, subprocessor list. Assembling it during a deal is what turns two days into five weeks. Treat a rescan failure as a production incident. A published listing pulled for a vulnerability blocks new subscribers immediately. Whoever owns your build pipeline should learn about it from monitoring, not from a customer. Rebuild on a schedule, not on demand. The AWS two-year AMI limit and the end-of-life rule mean a rebuild cadence is a compliance requirement, not hygiene. Ask about security review during qualification. One question — “who does your security review and how long does it usually take?” — sets the offer expiry realistically, which is the single most common cause of a reissued offer. Get custom terms drafted early if you need them. If your buyer’s security team always requires specific notification windows, standardise your own custom terms rather than negotiating them per deal. The listing readiness checklist covers what to have ready before the first deal rather than during it. Frequently asked questions Does a marketplace listing replace a buyer’s security review? No. Provider certification examines your artifact against marketplace policy. The buyer’s review examines your company’s controls, and it still happens. Can a listing be removed after it is published? Yes. AWS continuously rescans listings and may make a product unavailable to new subscribers, and Microsoft reserves the right to hide or deprecate a container offer with or without notice when vulnerabilities are found. What is the AWS vulnerability bar for machine images? AMIs must pass all security checks and must not contain critical or high-severity unpatched vulnerabilities or malware. End-of-life operating systems and software are not allowed. Do AMIs expire? Effectively. AWS states AMIs must not be older than two years from their creation date, so a stable product still needs a rebuild cadence. Must security incidents be reported to the marketplace? On Microsoft, yes. Policy 100.11 requires publishers to report suspected security events, including incidents and vulnerabilities, at the earliest opportunity. When does security review happen in a marketplace deal? Later and less predictably than in a direct deal, because commercial terms are often agreed first. Ask during qualification and set the offer expiry accordingly. Takeaways Two separate reviews run on every marketplace deal: the provider checks your artifact, the buyer checks your company. Provider certification is continuous. A listing that passed can be pulled later when a dependency ages out. AWS bars critical and high-severity unpatched vulnerabilities, end-of-life software, and machine images older than two years. Microsoft requires publishers to report suspected security events at the earliest opportunity — a duty separate from your customer contracts. The buyer’s questionnaire is about your controls, and no listing answers it. Publish the evidence before you are asked. Ask who runs security review during qualification, then set the offer expiry to survive it. Security review is a scheduling problem more often than a technical one. See how Suger’s agreement and terms management keeps custom terms, standardised terms and their approval state attached to the deal, so the security conversation starts with the right document.

title: Early Menopause May Raise the Risk of High Blood Pressure, New Study Finds
