title: Corrective vs Preventive Action in Software Engineering
summary: Learn the key differences between corrective and preventive action in software. Struct automates root-cause analysis & incident verification.
body_text: Written by: Nimesh Chakravarthi, Co-founder & CTO, Struct Key Takeaways for Engineering Leaders Correction stops immediate harm during an incident, corrective action removes the root cause after a confirmed failure, and preventive action removes risk before any failure occurs. Corrective action is reactive and begins after a production failure. Preventive action is proactive and starts when risk signals or trends appear. A complete CAPA flow for software teams uses seven steps and ends with automated incident resolution verification that confirms the failure mode is gone through observability data. Real-world incident pairs show how a single root cause can trigger corrective actions on the affected system and preventive actions that protect similar systems through CI gates and policy changes. Struct automates root-cause analysis and incident resolution verification for both corrective and preventive loops. Automate your on-call runbook to reclaim engineer-hours lost to manual triage. Timing Difference Between Corrective and Preventive Actions Corrective action is reactive and starts after a production failure is confirmed. Preventive action is proactive and starts when a risk signal appears before any failure occurs. ISO 9001:2015 Clause 10.2 requires organizations to react to nonconformities, evaluate their causes, implement appropriate actions, and review effectiveness. Preventive thinking is no longer a standalone clause. ISO 9001:2015 eliminated Preventive Action as a standalone requirement and distributed it across Clauses 4, 6, and 10 as risk-based thinking. For engineering teams, your on-call runbook must handle both loops: a post-incident corrective loop triggered by alert data and a proactive preventive loop triggered by trend analysis, error-rate drift, or near-miss signals from observability dashboards. Seven-Step CAPA Flow with Resolution Verification A complete CAPA flow for software teams closes only when observability data confirms the failure mode is gone, not when the ticket is marked done. There is no single common verification window for CAPA effectiveness . Teams choose periods based on risk and process frequency, often from weeks to 12 months, and confirm via objective evidence such as trends or repeat nonconformances. The following seven-step flow applies to every production incident your team investigates: Detection: An alert fires in Slack or PagerDuty, and the system records timestamp, impacted services, and blast radius. Containment (Correction): Roll back, turn off a feature flag, or reroute traffic to stop user impact immediately. Root-Cause Analysis: Use 5 Whys or fishbone analysis to trace the causal chain from symptom to systemic cause. Action Definition: Classify each output as corrective action that stops recurrence of this failure or preventive action that stops first occurrence on similar systems. Implementation: Ship code changes, update runbooks, adjust alert thresholds, or modify deploy gates with named owners and due dates. Incident Resolution Verification: Automatically check observability data such as error rates, latency percentiles, and saturation metrics to confirm the failure mode is absent, not just that the ticket is closed. Closure and Continuous Improvement: Archive the RCA, update the runbook, and feed risk signals into the preventive action backlog per ISO 9001:2015 Clause 10.3 . Step 6, incident resolution verification, is the most commonly skipped step. Verified closure treats “action complete” and “action effective” as two separate events . Teams must gather independent evidence that the deviation has not recurred at the same control point. The following three incident pairs show how this seven-step CAPA flow works in practice and how one root cause can drive both corrective and preventive actions. Three Paired Production-Incident Examples in Practice Each pair below shows one corrective and one preventive action drawn from real-style software incidents, structured by trigger, root cause, action taken, and verification outcome. Pair 1 — Database Connection Pool Exhaustion A silent config-library default change reduced the database connection pool from 100 to 10, causing checkout p99 latency to exceed 30 seconds within three minutes of deploy. The corrective action reverted the config default and added a saturation alert on pool utilization. Verification confirmed p99 returned below 500 ms within one deploy cycle. The preventive action added a CI gate that fails any config change touching connection pool defaults without an explicit reviewer sign-off, preventing first occurrence on all other services sharing the library. Pair 2 — Kubernetes Pod OOM Storm A Kubernetes pod OOM storm caused cascading restarts across a payment namespace. The corrective action patched the memory leak and adjusted pod memory limits. Verification showed zero OOM events over a 30-day monitoring window. The preventive action added a memory-based autoscaler rule and a CI memory regression test, blocking the same class of change from reaching production on any namespace. Pair 3 — Serverless Cold-Start Latency Breach Lazy-loading failures in a serverless function caused p99 invocation latency to breach SLA thresholds. The corrective action performed lazy-loading of libraries and reduced initialization work. Synthetic canaries validated improvement over 14 days. The preventive action enforced image size budgets and CI checks across all Lambda functions, stopping the same latency pattern from appearing in functions not yet affected. How ISO 9001:2015 Handles Prevention Today ISO 9001:2015 replaced the formal preventive action clause from the 2008 version with risk-based thinking because the committee recognized that good preventive thinking should sit inside every process, not in a separate procedure. Prevention now appears across Clauses 4.1 (context), 6.1 (planning actions to address risks), and 10.2 (corrective action feeding back into risk registers. For engineering teams, this shift has a direct operational implication. Under the 2008 version, the preventive action clause often resulted in empty folders at audit because it required documenting actions against problems that had not yet occurred. The 2015 model instead requires your team to show that risk signals such as error-rate trends, near-miss alerts, and dependency health scores actively feed your planning and deploy processes, not a backlog ticket labeled “someday.” Using 5 Whys and Fishbone for Root Cause The 5 Whys traces a single causal chain from symptom to systemic cause. The fishbone diagram maps contributing factors across multiple categories at the same time. Most software teams combine a timeline with the 5 Whys and then use a fishbone when the incident is multi-factor. Using the connection pool incident from Pair 1, a 5 Whys analysis runs as follows: Why did checkout latency spike? The database rejected new connections. Why did the database reject connections? The pool was exhausted at 10 connections. Why was the pool limited to 10? A config library update changed the default silently. Why did the update ship without review? No CI gate checked connection pool config diffs. Why did no gate exist? The team had never instrumented pool saturation as a deploy signal. A fishbone analysis of the same incident maps contributing factors across four categories: Process: No config-diff review step in the deploy checklist. Tooling: No saturation alert on connection pool utilization. People: Library update authored by a team without database context. Environment: Staging pool size masked the default change under lower load. The corrective action addresses the process and tooling categories. The preventive action, a CI gate blocking pool-config changes, addresses the systemic gap that would affect every service using the library. How Struct Automates Investigation and Verification The root-cause analysis step in the CAPA flow is where most engineering teams lose 30–45 minutes per incident. Struct removes that manual investigation window. When an alert fires in your Slack or PagerDuty channel, Struct immediately correlates logs from Datadog, AWS CloudWatch, Sentry, and GitHub to produce a root-cause output in under 10 minutes, before your on-call engineer opens their laptop. This 80%+ reduction in triage time, from 30 minutes to 2 minutes per incident, reclaims 56 engineer-hours per month across 2,100+ automated investigations. The root-cause step feeding both your corrective and preventive action workflows no longer acts as a bottleneck. Struct’s Incident Tracker, launched August 3, 2026, extends this automation to the verification step by running an approximately one-minute loop against your observability data to confirm an incident is actually resolved, not just acknowledged. The system checks error rates, latency percentiles, and saturation metrics continuously until the failure mode is absent, then closes the loop automatically. For the preventive side of the CAPA loop, Struct’s Deploy Guard operates at the PR level, running instrumentation review and post-deploy health checks before a bad change reaches production. Struct sits on top of your existing observability stack such as Datadog, Grafana, and Sentry as an investigation layer. It does not replace those tools. It automates the manual triage work that happens between alert and resolution. See how Struct eliminates manual triage and stop burning engineer-hours on root-cause steps that a purpose-built system can complete in minutes. For more on how engineering teams structure incident workflows, see the Incident Tracking & Resolution Verification hub and the Incident Response & Management hub . Frequently Asked Questions What is the simplest way to distinguish corrective action from preventive action? The trigger provides the simplest distinction. If a failure has already occurred and you are eliminating its root cause to stop recurrence, that is corrective action. If a risk signal, trend, or near-miss has appeared and you are acting before any failure occurs, that is preventive action. The timing of the trigger, after failure versus before failure, separates the two. Who owns corrective and preventive actions on an engineering team? Corrective actions should be owned by the engineer or team closest to the system that failed, with a named individual, a due date, and a SMART definition of done. Preventive actions often require cross-functional ownership because they address systemic gaps such as deploy pipelines, alert thresholds, or CI gates that span multiple teams. Engineering leadership is responsible for ensuring both action types have owners and are tracked to verified closure, not just ticket completion. How do you verify that a corrective action actually worked? Verification requires objective observability evidence, not a date-based review. Check that the specific failure mode, such as the error rate, latency breach, or saturation event, has not recurred over a defined window, typically 7–30 days of production traffic. A corrective action is not closed until that evidence exists. Struct’s Incident Tracker automates this verification loop by continuously checking your observability data against the incident’s failure signature and confirming resolution without manual follow-up. Can the same root cause produce both a corrective and a preventive action? Yes, and it should. The corrective action addresses the system that already failed. The preventive action extends the same fix, or a related one, to similar systems, services, or configurations that share the root cause but have not yet failed. A connection pool fix on one service becomes a CI gate that protects all services. A memory limit adjustment on one Kubernetes namespace becomes an autoscaler rule applied cluster-wide. How does Struct fit into an existing CAPA workflow? Struct automates Step 3 of the CAPA flow, root-cause analysis, by correlating logs, traces, metrics, and code context the moment an alert fires. It outputs a root-cause summary and suggested fixes within minutes, giving your team a verified starting point for defining corrective and preventive actions. Struct also handles incident resolution verification automatically by confirming through live observability data that the failure mode is gone before the incident is closed. Setup takes under 10 minutes and connects to Datadog, Sentry, AWS CloudWatch, GCP Logs, GitHub, and your existing Slack alerting channels. What metrics indicate that corrective and preventive actions are working? Track repeat incident rate, the number of incidents sharing the same root cause within a 90-day window divided by total incidents. A rate below 5% indicates strong follow-through on corrective actions. Also track MTTR trend over 30, 60, and 90 days. If corrective actions are effective, average investigation time should decrease. Struct’s 80%+ triage-time reduction, from 30-minute to 2-minute investigations, provides a concrete benchmark for what automated root-cause analysis can deliver against these metrics. What is incident resolution verification and why does it matter? Incident resolution verification is the automated process of confirming that an incident is genuinely resolved by checking live observability data, not by marking a ticket done. Without it, teams close incidents based on the absence of new alerts rather than evidence that the failure mode is gone. This pattern causes recurring incidents and inflated MTTR. Struct’s Incident Tracker runs a continuous verification loop against your observability stack and closes incidents only when the data confirms the failure signature has cleared. This closed-loop step separates a complete CAPA workflow from one that produces documentation without preventing recurrence. Every manual root-cause investigation your team runs is time not spent shipping product. Struct removes the 30–45 minute manual investigation window, automates incident resolution verification, and feeds both your corrective and preventive action workflows with evidence-backed root-cause outputs. Book a demo to reclaim your team’s triage hours and stop losing engineer-hours to manual investigation today.

title: Building Lasting Relationships in Freight: Troy Shasko on Service and Staying Driven
summary: In our latest Landstar agent profile, Troy Shasko shares how experience, integrity, discipline and a relationship-first mindset have shaped his approach for decades.
body_text: In the Landstar network, success is often built over time—through relationships, consistency and a commitment to doing the right thing. For Troy Shasko, that mindset has helped shape a long-standing independent Landstar agency focused on customer trust and operational strength. With decades in the business, Shasko has grown his family-based agency by combining hands-on industry experience with an entrepreneurial drive, emphasizing accountability, communication and service at every step. In this Landstar agent profile, you’ll learn: Why long-term relationships are central to sustained growth How Landstar’s network supports expansion across modes and markets What it takes to build a reputation rooted in service and consistency Why an entrepreneurial mindset still matters—no matter how long you’ve been in the business Building capabilities through long-term relationships Based in Belle Vernon, Pennsylvania, Shasko Team Logistics has built a reputation for delivering transportation solutions with some of the most respected names in retail, manufacturing, energy, and heavy haul project logistics for decades. Since joining the family business in 1986, Troy Shasko has helped grow an agency that has been part of the Landstar network since its early years. Today, the agency supports customers across multiple modes, including contract truckload, hazmat, heavy haul, cross-border freight (Mexico and Canada) and time-sensitive shipments, with a significant portion of the business focused on high-value contract freight and heavy haul project logistics, with an emphasis on delivering consistent service and maintaining long-term customer relationships. Shasko’s project logistics experience includes planning and coordinating complex, multi-phase transportation programs for large-scale construction and industrial projects. Building the foundation: experience, integrity and follow-through From his early days working on loading docks to serving as a U.S. Army logistics and aviation officer, Shasko developed a practical understanding of freight and operations before entering the agency business. That foundation helped shape a straightforward approach to business: Do the right thing Follow through on commitments Treat customers and operators with respect and care Over time, that approach has helped foster long-term relationships with customers who have worked with the agency for years. For Shasko, that consistency starts with a simple leadership principle: “Be a great team player and lead your team.” What helped most: leveraging the Landstar network and relationships As the agency grew, Shasko emphasized the importance of working closely with both Landstar’s corporate resources and network of owner-operators. Doing so helped build capacity and allowed the agency to pursue new opportunities in complex modes and services. And, over time, that collaboration has led to his agency’s reputation for consistent service, with some operators supporting specific lanes for many years. The combination of relationships, tools and network support has helped his agency deliver the safety, security and service customers expect. For one year-long project, Shasko’s team helped coordinate more than 3,300 truckload shipments, including more than 1,100 over-dimensional heavy haul truckloads, along with expedited, LTL, ocean and air shipments moving from multiple U.S. states and international origins. The agency’s support helped the team complete the project both on time and on budget. Think like an owner: the mindset behind long-term success For Shasko, success comes back to mentality. He emphasizes the importance of staying driven and continually earning your place on the team. “I fire myself at the end of every day and work to improve and earn my position back the next day” he says—a reflection of the entrepreneurial mindset that continues to guide the agency. His advice for new agents Be driven. Approach each day with urgency and accountability. Do the right thing. Integrity and follow-through build long-term trust. Hustle daily. Engage with every opportunity and learn the business. Build relationships . Strong connections with customers, owner-operators and corporate teams support growth. FAQ: Becoming a Landstar Freight Agent 1. What does a Landstar freight agent do? A Landstar freight agent is an independent business owner who builds customer relationships and arranges transportation solutions while leveraging the Landstar network and resources to help move freight and communicate the results quickly. 2. How does Landstar support freight agents? Support includes access to technology, operations and an established capacity network that helps agents meet customer needs and expand capabilities. 3. What advice does Shasko give for long-term success as an agent? For Shasko, long-term success comes from consistency, relationship-building, follow-through and a strong work ethic rooted in discipline and integrity. He points to a Lou Holtz quote as a reminder of the mindset required to sustain success: “Ability is what you’re capable of doing. Motivation determines what you do. Attitude determines how well you do it.”

title: One GTM Motion Across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
summary: The operating model for running AWS, Azure and Google Cloud marketplaces as one motion: what standardises cleanly, and what never abstracts away.
body_text: Running one go-to-market motion across AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud means standardising the parts that are genuinely the same — the deal record, the entitlement state, the revenue trail — and refusing to abstract the parts that are not. Teams that get the boundary wrong in either direction pay for it, just differently. Adding the second marketplace usually costs about what the first did. That is expected, and forgivable. Adding the third costing the same is the signal that something structural is wrong. By then a team has seen enough of the pattern to have generalised it, and if the cost is flat it means nothing was generalised — each marketplace is a separate programme with its own spreadsheet, its own definition of “active customer,” and its own person who knows how it works. The opposite failure is quieter and worse: a single abstraction that pretends the three clouds are one, and produces offers that are subtly wrong on two of them. The useful question is not “can this be unified” but “which layer is actually common.” What is the same everywhere Three things generalise cleanly across every marketplace, because they describe your business rather than the provider’s process. The deal record. A negotiated deal has a customer, a value, a term, a set of entitlements and an approval state. None of that is cloud-specific. If your CRM holds one shape of marketplace deal, every marketplace can be generated from it. Entitlement state. What a customer is entitled to right now is a property of your product, not of the marketplace that sold it. Every cloud gives you a way to read authoritative state; the answer they return means the same thing. Build one internal model and populate it from three sources. The revenue trail. Booked, invoiced, disbursed, reconciled. The vocabulary and the timing differ per cloud, but the questions finance asks do not. One normalised ledger, three adapters. Standardise these and the third marketplace genuinely is cheaper than the first, because the only new work is an adapter. What never abstracts The acceptance path is different on each cloud, in ways that change what you promise a customer. This is where a single abstraction quietly lies. AWS: the offer is the unit, and change means replacement. An agreement is an accepted offer. Changing one means an amendment, and “an amendment replaces a buyer’s current subscription” — remaining scheduled payments are cancelled and replaced by whatever schedule the amendment carries. There is one buyer-facing act: accept. Microsoft: four acts, four failure points. Accept, purchase, subscribe, activate. Each needs different permissions. Purchasing requires “an Azure subscription owner or contributor role for a subscription under the billing account of the private offer,” and the offer itself “aligns to your billing account.” There is a real delay in the middle — 15 to 60 minutes after acceptance before the Purchase button enables — and a real deadline at the end, with buyers asked to ensure “the partner activates your SaaS subscription within 30 days after purchase.” Google Cloud: the purchase sits alongside the customer’s cloud spending. “For most configurations, your customers receive one bill for all of your products and services, as well as the Google Cloud services that they use,” across SaaS, VM images, Kubernetes apps, data products and professional services. Two defaults differ enough to matter commercially. Microsoft SaaS subscriptions have auto-renew off by default. AWS public offers auto-renew, but “if you amend an accepted public offer, it becomes a private offer and no longer auto-renews.” A renewal forecast built on one cloud’s default will be wrong on the other. The co-sell layer diverges further still — how co-sell works covers the three programmes separately for exactly that reason. Where to put the seams The design that holds is a common core with thin, honest adapters: Layer Common or per-cloud Deal record and approval Common Offer construction Common inputs, per-cloud rendering Acceptance and activation Per-cloud, always Entitlement state Common model, per-cloud source Metering submission Per-cloud, with common validation Revenue and reconciliation Common ledger, per-cloud adapter Renewal tracking Common, with per-cloud defaults encoded The rule that keeps this honest: an adapter may translate, but it may never invent. If Microsoft requires a billing account identifier and your common deal record has no field for it, the fix is a field on the deal record — not a default inside the adapter. Defaults inside adapters are how a team ends up with offers targeted at the wrong tenant and no idea which layer chose it. The four questions that reveal whether you have one motion Ask these of your own team. Each takes a minute to answer if the model is unified and a week if it is not. How many marketplace agreements end in the next 90 days, across everything? If the answer requires three exports, renewals are three programmes. What is the total value of what we sold through marketplaces last quarter? If each cloud reports a different definition of “sold,” you have three ledgers. Which customers are entitled to the enterprise tier right now? If the answer depends on which cloud they bought through, the entitlement model is per-cloud. Who owns the fourth marketplace? If nobody can start one without a new headcount, the model has not generalised. Suger transacts on six marketplaces, and the reason the sixth is not six times the work is entirely this: one deal record, one entitlement model, one ledger, and adapters that translate rather than decide. The sequencing that works Normalise before you automate. Automating three different processes gives you three automations to maintain. Agree what a marketplace deal is first. Make entitlement state authoritative before anything reads it. Every downstream consumer — provisioning, support, renewals, finance — should read one model. Entitlement management on cloud marketplaces covers the state machine underneath it. Encode the per-cloud defaults explicitly. Auto-renew behaviour, activation deadlines and permission requirements belong in code with a comment naming the cloud, not in a person’s memory. Reconcile across all of them on the same schedule. Drift found per-cloud is three investigations; drift found against one ledger is one. Marketplace revenue reconciliation covers the mechanics. Frequently asked questions Can one process really cover every cloud marketplace? The deal record, entitlement model and revenue ledger can be common. Acceptance, activation and metering cannot — each provider implements them differently, and pretending otherwise produces offers that are wrong on at least one cloud. What is the most common mistake when unifying? Putting defaults in the adapter. When a cloud requires a field the common model lacks, add it to the model rather than letting the adapter choose a value nobody can trace. Do renewals behave the same across clouds? No. Microsoft SaaS subscriptions default to auto-renew off, and on AWS an amended public offer becomes a private offer and stops auto-renewing. Encode each default rather than assuming one. Why does the third marketplace cost as much as the first? Because nothing was generalised after the first two. If each marketplace has its own spreadsheet and its own definition of an active customer, every addition is a new programme. What should be standardised first? Entitlement state. It has the most downstream consumers — provisioning, support, renewals and finance — so unifying it pays back fastest. How do you tell whether the motion is really unified? Ask how many agreements end in the next 90 days across every marketplace. If answering needs three exports, it is not one motion. Takeaways The deal record, entitlement state and revenue ledger generalise cleanly. Standardise those and the next marketplace is an adapter. Acceptance and activation never generalise. AWS has one buyer act, Microsoft has four with different permissions, Google Cloud folds the purchase into the customer’s cloud bill. Renewal defaults differ by cloud, so a single forecast assumption will be wrong somewhere. An adapter may translate but must never invent. Missing fields belong on the common model. Unify entitlement state first — it has the most downstream consumers. If answering “what ends in 90 days” takes three exports, you have three programmes rather than one motion. The point of one motion is that the next marketplace is a decision, not a project. See how the Suger platform runs listings, offers, entitlements and revenue across every marketplace from one model, with the per-cloud differences handled where they belong.

title: AWS Clean Rooms supports exporting privacy-enhanced analysis logs for SQL
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with AWS Clean Rooms supports exporting privacy-enhanced analysis logs for SQL
body_text: AWS Clean Rooms now supports exporting privacy-enhanced analysis logs for SQL analyses , offering customers greater optimization and troubleshooting capabilities. With this launch, you can export privacy-enhanced analysis logs to an S3 bucket for SQL queries that ran in an AWS Clean Rooms collaboration, providing insight into Spark execution details that can help you optimize and troubleshoot your queries. Collaboration owners grant a member the ability to export analysis logs when they create a collaboration or submit a change request to grant the ability to a member of an existing collaboration. After a query runs, you can export the privacy-enhanced analysis logs to your desired S3 path. For example, a third-party measurement provider collaborating with a publisher can identify an anomalous data skew that is causing a query to run slower than usual, accelerating time-to-resolution and optimizing costs. AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms .

title: What’s new in Power Platform: July/August 2026 feature update
summary: Get the latest news in Power Platform from the last month, so you can find a summary of product, community, and learning updates from Power Platform in one easy place.
body_text: Summary Welcome to the Power Platform monthly feature update! We will use this blog to share news in Power Platform from the last month, so you can find a summary of product, community, and learning updates from Power Platform in one easy place. Now, let’s dive into what’s new in Power Platform: Get started with the latest updates today! Jump into Power Apps, Power Automate, and Power Pages to try the latest updates, you can use an existing environment or get started for free using the Developer plan. Developer plan Power Apps Power Automate Power Pages Join us at PPCC! See these updates and more come to life at the Power Platform Community Conference 2026 – Join us October 27-29 at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas to discover how organizations are using agents, apps, and automations to drive business outcomes, build new solutions, and scale innovation. Connect with product experts, industry peers, and the community shaping what’s next. Register today Building modern apps Generally available: the data grid modern control — a fluent UI grid with search, sorting, selection, and rich column types The data grid modern control is now generally available for canvas apps. Built on fluent UI, data grid gives makers a high-performance, data-dense view of tabular data with a built-in search experience. Columns are generated automatically when you connect a data source, and each column can be unlocked for per-column customization with Power Fx formulas . GA rounds out the core interaction model: sortable columns, single and multi-row selection (with an optional selection column), column resizing , and a rich set of column types — text, number, phone, email, hyperlink , and button columns — plus formula-driven cell content for lookups, images, and complex fields. The control ships with built-in accessibility (keyboard navigation and screen-reader support) and fluent theming that stays consistent with the rest of your app, and it now works across a broader range of data sources than the preview. A wave of reliability and authoring fixes (selection stability, sorting, column ordering, and data-grid-in-gallery/component scenarios) landed as part of the GA push. Data grid is the fluent-based successor to the classic table/data table experience, and a table → data grid update path helps makers move existing apps forward rather than rebuilding. It’s a distinct new control, not a forced replacement. Learn more Modern toggle and checkbox get improvements with consistent properties, tooltips, and true read-only view mode The modern toggle and checkbox controls have been improved as part of modern controls. Both now follow the same cross-control naming conventions as the rest of the modern set — FontColor → Color , FontSize → Size , and the FontItalic/Underline/Strikethrough renames — and FontWeight now uses typed enum values ( FontWeight.Bold , etc.) for IntelliSense and compile-time validation. Toggle’s LabelPosition is also now a typed enum ( LabelPosition.Before / LabelPosition.After ). Both controls gain a new tooltip property, and DisplayMode.View now renders a genuinely read-only state that shows the value without allowing interaction — consistent with the other updated modern controls. They also expose far more output properties than the previous versions, so you can reference their state in formulas across your app. Checkbox behavior inside galleries (Checked/OnCheck reliability) is improved. If your app uses a previous version, you’ll see an update notification on the control in Power Apps studio; the migration guide lists each property rename so you can update formula references. Learn more The modern form control gets modern data cards plus binding, formula, and reset fixes for more reliable form building The modern form experience received a round of functional improvements . Improved data cards are now enabled, so forms built on modern controls render their fields through the updated data-card infrastructure. Alongside that, we fixed data-card binding and formula behavior, so field values, defaults, and Power Fx inside cards evaluate correctly. This makes modern forms behave predictably for real data-entry scenarios. We also corrected ResetForm and date picker reset behavior: resetting a form now reliably clears and restores field values, including date fields, which is core to edit/new-record form lifecycles. Together these changes make the modern form a dependable foundation for form-driven canvas apps, working end to end with the other updated modern controls. Learn more New fluent 2 app templates give makers a polished, modern-controls starting point for canvas apps Makers now have new fluent 2-based templates that provide a ready-to-use, professionally designed starting point for canvas apps — built on modern controls and fluent patterns instead of a blank screen. New screen templates include a hub landing page , a feature landing page , and a list page , and the existing modern gallery templates were refreshed to use modern controls throughout. Because the templates are assembled from the modern control set, apps you start from them inherit consistent fluent theming, built-in accessibility, and the ongoing quality investment in modern controls — so makers get a good-looking, maintainable app faster. New and improved modern controls: a rating control, richer text styling for card, and an expanded 180-icon library The modern controls catalog also grew and got richer. A brand-new rating modern control (built on fluent UI v9) lets users give star-based ratings with half-star precision , custom icons (not just stars), and full color customization defaulting to your app’s brand color. It’s a new control — classic rating keeps working unchanged. The card control gained text-customization properties — fill , plus TitleColor / SubtitleColor / DescriptionColor and TitleSize / SubtitleSize / DescriptionSize. The modern icon control’s library was expanded from ~56 to ~180 icons , reaching parity with the classic icon set. Classic icon.* values are automatically mapped to their fluent equivalents, so existing usage lights up with the broader set. Deprecating older fluent UI (hero) controls in custom pages and Teams apps and their upgrade path to the modern controls Makers who built with the earlier fluent UI (“hero”) controls in custom pages and Teams apps now have a documented upgrade path to the modern controls . The guidance explains how the upgrade works, which properties carry over, and where behavior differs, so you can move to the actively-invested modern control set with confidence. Because some hero properties don’t have a one-to-one equivalent on the modern controls (for example certain color/theming settings), the guidance is explicit about what transfers and what to check after upgrading — reducing surprises and protecting maker trust during migration. Modern controls are the forward path for canvas and custom-page authoring, while classic controls remain supported for organizations with their own design systems. Learn more Power Automate Share process license capacity across multiple flows with flow groups Flow groups are now available in Power Automate. They let you share the capacity of one process license, or 250,000 actions per day, across up to 25 solution-aware cloud flows, helping you make better use of capacity across flows with moderate, predictable usage. Go to more > flow groups to create a group, add flows, and monitor shared capacity. A flow group uses one process license. When a flow needs more capacity, you can assign process licenses directly to that flow for dedicated capacity. Share process license capacity with flow groups Learn more Build and manage cloud flows from your AI coding agent with the Power Automate plugin The Power Automate plugin is now available in the Power Platform skills marketplace for GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code. It brings common Power Automate tasks into your terminal, so you can create, edit, run, and debug cloud flows through a natural language conversation. Ask the plugin to build a flow from a description, update an existing flow, investigate a failed run, or help select a working environment and manage connections. Review and test generated definitions and changes before you enable or publish a flow. Learn more Power Pages Public preview: secure your Power Pages sites with the new security agent Security agent (preview) is a new AI-powered assistant built into the Power Pages security workspace that helps makers review, configure, and strengthen site security using natural language. Whether you’re reviewing your site’s security posture, configuring authentication and authorization, managing application security settings, or troubleshooting sign-in issues, security agent provides site-specific guidance based on your current configuration. The agent explains findings in plain language, recommends remediation steps, and always requests your approval before making configuration changes, helping you secure your sites faster while staying in control. title: Expense Policy Reinforcement: Turning Rules into Everyday Behaviour
summary: Learn how to reinforce your expense policy. Discover ways to build compliance, automate approvals, and turn rules into everyday behaviour across teams.
body_text: You may have a written expense policy, but if your team still files late claims, submits weak receipts, or routinely breaches the rules, then the policy is not driving the behaviour you need. Expense policy reinforcement is not simply about having a document; it’s about making it a behaviour-shaping, accountability-driving system that your organisation follows in practice. For finance leaders, the challenge is clear: turn rules into everyday behaviour so that policies aren’t just written, but followed, enforced, and improved over time. This requires a blend of clear policy design, practical workflows, and systems that reinforce compliance, not only at the point of reimbursement but throughout the entire spend lifecycle. In this article, you’ll learn how to build and reinforce expense policies that improve control, reduce disputes, and scale with your business goals. Key Takeaways Reinforcement drives compliance: Expense policies are effective only when consistently applied; real behaviour change matters more than policy length. Clarity reduces friction: Defined rules, limits, and approval flows make adherence predictable and reduce confusion across departments. Automation builds discipline: Embedding controls at the point of spend and approval ensures compliance happens naturally, not manually. Monitoring keeps policies relevant: Regular reviews and data-driven insights ensure expense rules evolve with business growth and regulatory updates. Consistency creates culture: Reinforced policies turn compliance into everyday behaviour, building accountability across the organisation. Why Expense Policies Break Down Without Reinforcement Most expense policies fail in practice, not because they lack detail, but because they aren’t embedded into the actual behaviours of employees and managers. A policy can sit on a drive or intranet, but without reinforcement, it becomes a reference document, not a control mechanism. From your perspective in finance, weak enforcement leads to: Unclear spending behaviour , where teams interpret rules differently and inconsistently. Delayed approvals , which slow reporting and create cash–flow ambiguity. Higher error rates , with missing receipts and misclassification. Risk of compliance issues such as incorrect VAT claims, late filings, or audit red flags. Many organisations write their expense policies with checklists and limits, but later discover that employees ignore or bypass them because the policies are difficult to follow or lack real-time accountability. In your role, reinforcing policy means the rules must be both clear and supported by processes that make following the policy the path of least resistance. This requires visibility, automation, and continuous monitoring, not annual reminders. As you refine your expense policy, the goal should be simple: make compliance easy and desirable, and non-compliance costly in terms of time, approval delays, or visibility. Defining the Purpose and Scope of Your Expense Policy Expense policy reinforcement starts with clarity. If the purpose and scope of your policy are not clearly defined, enforcement becomes inconsistent and subjective. Clarifying the Purpose of the Policy Your expense policy should clearly state why it exists . From a finance perspective, the purpose typically includes: Protecting company funds from misuse or leakage Ensuring consistent treatment of expenses across teams Supporting accurate financial reporting and VAT compliance Improving visibility and accountability for business spending When this purpose is explicit, employees understand that the policy is not administrative paperwork, but a control framework that supports financial discipline. Identifying Who the Policy Applies To Reinforcement weakens when it is unclear who must follow the policy. You should clearly define whether it applies to: Full-time employees Contractors or consultants Temporary staff or third parties authorised to spend As organisations scale, roles change quickly. Clear applicability avoids disputes and ensures consistent enforcement regardless of seniority or department. Defining the Types of Expenses Covered Your policy should also specify which expense categories are governed. This often includes: Travel and accommodation Meals and client entertainment Subscriptions and software tools Operational and project-related purchases Clear scope reduces assumptions, prevents misuse, and ensures everyone operates within the same financial boundaries. For a deeper look at why clarity at this stage matters, read our guide on why your business needs a detailed expense policy . Drawing Clear Lines Between Reimbursable and Non-Reimbursable Expenses Ambiguity around reimbursements is one of the fastest ways to undermine an expense policy. Reinforcement depends on removing guesswork from the process. Clearly Defining Reimbursable Expenses Your policy should outline which expenses are eligible for reimbursement, such as: Pre-approved business travel within set limits Client meetings aligned with company guidelines Essential operational purchases made for work purposes Providing examples helps employees self-assess claims before submission, reducing unnecessary back-and-forth. Listing Non-Reimbursable Expenses Explicitly Non-reimbursable expenses should be equally clear. Common examples include: Personal purchases or upgrades Expenses submitted outside the defined timelines Claims without valid receipts or documentation Spend that falls outside approved categories Explicit exclusions strengthen reinforcement by setting firm boundaries. Reducing Disputes Through Clarity From a finance standpoint, clear reimbursement rules: Reduce approval delays Minimise policy disputes Improve data accuracy in accounting systems Support consistent VAT treatment When employees know what will and will not be reimbursed, compliance becomes predictable rather than reactive. Clear boundaries reduce disputes, speed up approvals, and help employees self-check claims before submission. If you’re refining reimbursement rules, this guide on small business expense reimbursement policy best practices is a useful reference. Setting Spend Limits That Balance Control and Flexibility Spend limits play a critical role in reinforcing your expense policy. When limits are unclear or unrealistic, employees either bypass them or constantly request exceptions, both of which weaken control. Establishing Category-Wise Limits and Per Diems Your policy should define spending caps by category, such as: Daily meal allowances Hotel and travel limits Client entertainment thresholds Software and subscription spending Category-wise limits provide guardrails without requiring case-by-case intervention from finance teams. Aligning Limits with Business Reality Reinforcement fails when limits are disconnected from how your teams actually work. You should review: Market rates in regions where employees operate Role-specific needs, such as sales versus operations Frequency of travel or client-facing activities When limits reflect real conditions, compliance improves naturally because employees are not forced to work around the policy. Defining a Clear Exception Process Even well-designed limits require flexibility. Your policy should clearly explain: When exceptions are allowed Who can approve them How they should be documented A transparent exception process reinforces discipline by making flexibility structured rather than informal. Spend limits are most effective when they reflect real business needs rather than static assumptions, especially as teams scale or operate across regions. For practical examples of how limits and rules are structured, see our sample guide on creating a business expense policy . Documentation and Receipt Rules That Actually Get Followed Receipt requirements are often where expense policies break down. Strict rules without practical execution lead to missing documentation and delayed claims. Specifying Required Supporting Documents Your policy should clearly state what documentation is required for each expense type, including: Itemised tax invoices Vendor details and transaction dates VAT breakdowns where applicable This clarity reduces rejected claims and repeated follow-ups. Defining Accepted Formats and Timelines Reinforcement improves when expectations are simple. Your policy should specify: Accepted formats, such as digital receipts or invoices Submission deadlines to prevent delayed claims Consequences for missing or late documentation Clear timelines encourage timely behaviour and cleaner month-end reporting. Linking Documentation to Compliance Requirements For UAE-based businesses, receipt rules should align with Federal Tax Authority requirements. Valid VAT invoices must include mandatory details such as the supplier’s TRN and VAT amount. When documentation standards are tied to compliance, employees better understand the importance of accuracy rather than viewing receipts as an administrative burden. Approval Workflows That Reinforce Policy, Not Slow Teams Down Approval workflows are where expense policies are tested in practice. If approvals are unclear or inconsistent, enforcement weakens, and teams lose confidence in the policy. Mapping the Submission and Approval Flow Your policy should clearly outline how an expense moves from submission to approval. This includes: How employees submit expenses The sequence of approvals required What happens when an expense is rejected or queried Clear workflows remove ambiguity and ensure expenses are reviewed consistently, regardless of department or role. Defining Approval Roles and Thresholds Reinforcement improves when approvals are role-based rather than ad hoc. Your policy should specify: Who approves expenses at different spend levels When a finance review is mandatory How seniority or department affects approval paths Defined thresholds reduce subjective decision-making and help managers approve faster with confidence. Using Automation to Maintain Consistency and Audit Trails Manual approvals often lead to delays and uneven enforcement. Automated workflows help ensure: Expenses are routed to the right approver every time Policy checks are applied consistently Audit trails are created automatically for reviews and audits For finance teams, this means stronger control without increasing administrative workload. Well-designed approval workflows reinforce accountability while keeping expenses moving without unnecessary delays. To explore this further in the context of travel and entertainment spend, read our guide on understanding corporate T&E policy and expense management. Standardising Expense Categorisation for Better Visibility and Control Expense categorisation is a foundational element of policy reinforcement. Without consistent categories, even compliant expenses become difficult to analyse and control. Aligning Categories with the Chart of Accounts Your policy should require employees to categorise expenses according to your chart of accounts. This ensures: Accurate financial reporting Easier reconciliation with accounting systems Cleaner data for audits and reviews Clear category definitions reduce misclassification and rework for finance teams. Improving Spend Analysis and Policy Monitoring When expenses are categorised consistently, you can: Track spend patterns by category and department Identify policy breaches or unusual trends early Assess whether limits and rules remain appropriate This visibility turns expense data into a reinforcement tool, not just a record. Supporting Tax Treatment and Deductibility Proper categorisation also supports correct tax treatment. Certain expense categories may be partially deductible, non-deductible, or VAT-recoverable. Standardisation helps ensure: Accurate VAT reporting Reduced compliance risk Better readiness for audits Integrating Expense Policies with Accounting and Payroll Systems An expense policy cannot be effectively reinforced if it operates in isolation. When expense data sits outside your accounting and payroll systems, gaps emerge that weaken visibility, accuracy, and control. Ensuring Seamless Data Flow Across Systems Your policy should clearly state that all approved expenses flow directly into your accounting system. This integration ensures: Expenses are recorded consistently and in real time Manual re-entry is eliminated Finance teams work with a single source of truth When systems are connected, policy compliance is reflected immediately in your books, not discovered weeks later. Supporting Audit Readiness and VAT Recovery Integrated systems make it easier to trace expenses from transaction to ledger. This is especially important for: Audit preparation VAT validation and recovery Ensuring expense claims meet documentation standards When expense data, receipts, and approvals are synced, finance teams can respond confidently to audits without last-minute reconciliation efforts. Reducing Errors and Manual Intervention Disconnected systems often lead to duplicate entries, mispostings, or delayed corrections. Integration reinforces policy by: Applying consistent rules across expense and accounting workflows Reducing human error Allowing finance teams to focus on oversight rather than data cleanup Turning Expense Policies into Everyday Behaviour Through Automation Reinforcement works best when compliance happens naturally, not through constant reminders or manual checks. Automation plays a central role in making expense policies part of everyday behaviour. Embedding Rules at the Point of Spend Automated controls allow policies to be enforced before money is spent, not after. This includes: Spend limits are applied in real time Vendor or category restrictions Automatic flagging of non-compliant transactions By guiding behaviour upfront, automation reduces violations without creating friction. Replacing Manual Reviews with Consistent Policy Checks Manual reviews are time-consuming and inconsistent. Automated checks ensure: Every expense is reviewed against the same rules Exceptions are flagged immediately Finance teams gain confidence in policy enforcement This consistency strengthens trust in the policy and the process. Reinforcing Accountability Without Micromanagement Automation shifts reinforcement from policing to visibility. Employees understand: What is allowed What will be flagged How approvals work This transparency encourages responsible spending while preserving autonomy. Automation closes the gap between policy intent and real-world behaviour by embedding controls directly into daily workflows. To see how this works in practice, read how Washmen put its spend management on autopilot and saved 80+ hours per week using Alaan . Educating Teams Without Creating Policy Fatigue Even the most well-designed expense policy will fail if employees see it as complex or restrictive. Reinforcement depends on helping teams understand why the policy exists and how to follow it with minimal effort. Communicating the Policy in Practical Ways Lengthy documents are rarely effective on their own. You should reinforce your expense policy through: Short, role-specific guidelines Clear examples tied to common spending scenarios Easy access to policy summaries when expenses are submitted When employees can quickly find answers, compliance improves without repeated clarification from finance teams. Providing Ongoing Guidance and Support Education should not be limited to onboarding. As policies evolve, reinforcement requires: Periodic refreshers when rules or limits change Clear communication around updates and reasons for change A defined point of contact for questions or edge cases This approach builds confidence and reduces unintentional policy breaches. Building Trust Through Transparency Employees are more likely to follow policies when enforcement feels fair and consistent. Transparency around approvals, rejections, and exceptions helps teams understand that rules apply equally across the organisation, regardless of role or seniority. Monitoring, Auditing, and Strengthening Policy Compliance Over Time Expense policy reinforcement is not a one-time exercise. As your business grows, spending patterns change, and policies must evolve to remain effective. Using Data to Monitor Compliance Trends Regular monitoring helps you identify: Repeat violations by category or department Unusual spending patterns Areas where policies may be unclear or outdated These insights allow finance teams to address root causes rather than reacting to individual claims. Conducting Regular Audits Without Disruption Audits should be structured and predictable, not reactive. A clear audit approach: Validates policy adherence Supports regulatory and VAT compliance Reinforces accountability without disrupting daily operations Consistent audits strengthen trust in both the policy and the finance function. Refining the Policy Based on Real Behaviour The strongest expense policies evolve. Use insights from monitoring and audits to: Adjust limits that no longer reflect reality Clarify ambiguous rules Strengthen controls where risk increases This continuous feedback loop ensures your policy remains relevant, enforceable, and aligned with business goals. How Alaan Supports Expense Policy Reinforcement in Practice Expense policy reinforcement depends on more than written rules. It requires systems that guide spending behaviour, apply controls consistently, and give finance teams real-time visibility. This is where Alaan supports finance leaders in practice. At Alaan , we provide an AI-powered spend and expense management platform designed for businesses in the UAE and wider MENA region. Our platform brings together corporate cards, expense automation, and accounting integrations to help you reinforce policies at scale. Configurable approval workflows that reflect your internal hierarchies and spending thresholds, ensuring consistent enforcement. VAT-aware receipt validation aligned with UAE Federal Tax Authority requirements, supporting accurate and compliant reporting. Real-time dashboards and insights that help you monitor adherence, identify exceptions, and refine policies using actual spend data. Trusted by more than 1,000 businesses across the UAE, from startups to large enterprises, Alaan helps finance teams save time, reduce errors, and gain complete visibility over company spending. At this stage, many finance leaders want to quantify the impact of stronger policy reinforcement rather than rely on assumptions. Conclusion Reinforcing your expense policy is about shaping everyday spending behaviour, not tightening rules after the fact. When policies are clear, supported by the right workflows, and reinforced through automation, compliance becomes part of how your teams operate, not an extra task they work around. For finance leaders, this approach delivers real value. You gain better visibility, fewer disputes, cleaner data, and stronger control as your business scales. More importantly, you move from reacting to policy breaches to preventing them altogether. title: What engineering teams look for in API integration platforms
summary: Ten things engineering teams check when evaluating API integration platforms, drawn from real customer calls.
body_text: Between January and August 2026, we talked to more than 300 engineering teams evaluating integration platforms for agentic and SaaS use cases. These were real buyers comparing Nango and other vendors for their customer-facing integrations. Most had already operated API integrations in production, and came with evaluation criteria centered on control, reliability, and security, learned from their own use cases. This post covers what teams look for in an API integration platform. The criteria apply to any platform in the category (agentic integrations, embedded iPaaS, unified APIs, SaaS integration platforms) and to infrastructure you build in-house. The criteria at a glance Criterion The question teams asked Control over integration logic Can we change an integration without waiting on your roadmap? Catalog depth What does "supported" cover for the APIs on our roadmap? Complete auth handling How do you detect revoked credentials, and what does re-auth look like? Reliability at scale What happens when a webhook is dropped or a backfill sync hits a limit? Debuggable observability Can we see every request for one customer's connection? Deployment and data residency Can this run in the EU, or inside our own cloud account? Security posture What does an attacker get if you are breached? Projectable pricing What does our usage shape cost at 10x? AI agent readiness Can agents call the integrations, and can coding agents build them? Exit path Could we leave without rewriting everything? The ten criteria engineering teams care about 1. Control over the integration logic The most common question across customer calls: what happens when the pre-built integration does not do what we need? Teams that had used pre-built unified APIs (Merge, Apideck, Finch) hit this wall on custom fields. Normalized data models cover less than you would expect. Salesforce and HubSpot contacts share only about five fields out of the box ; the data your product actually needs (deal conventions, custom objects, regional fields) lives outside the shared schema. What teams checked: Code access: Can you read and edit the integration logic itself, or only configure it? Roadmap independence: If a field or endpoint is missing, can your team add it the same week, or do you file a feature request and wait? The cost of workarounds: Raw API access matters, but if it is just a bare passthrough request, you own auth, retries, and rate limits again for that call. Why B2B SaaS teams outgrow pre-built unified APIs covers this failure mode in detail. Teams that overlooked this tended to come back 12 to 18 months later asking about migration paths. Migrations were the expensive failure mode in almost every story we heard. 2. Catalog depth Few teams asked how many APIs a platform supports in total. Most asked what “supported” means for each API on their roadmap. “Supported” can mean a full sync with pagination, rate-limit handling, and tests. It can also mean a logo and an auth flow. The gap between the two usually becomes visible only after you have committed. What teams checked: Per-provider depth: Which endpoints, objects, and auth modes does the integration actually cover? Long-tail turnaround: For an API the platform does not support yet, is the answer days, weeks, or “on the roadmap”? Self-serve extension: Can your team add a new provider without the vendor’s involvement? 3. Auth that is handled completely OAuth is nominally a standard. RFC 6749 itself warns that it is “likely to produce a wide range of non-interoperable implementations”, and that warning holds in practice: provider-specific parameters, token rotation policies, and unannounced breaking changes. Operating auth for 900+ APIs, we found that 16% of commits to our provider configurations are fixes for changes providers never announced. What teams checked: Token lifecycle: How are refresh race conditions and token rotation handled? With a rotation-enforcing provider, a small bug destroys connections permanently. Revocation detection: How does the platform know credentials stopped working before your customer tells you? Re-auth experience: When a user has to reconnect, what do they see, and whose brand is on it? Beyond OAuth: HR, finance, and ERP APIs often use API keys, client credentials, or custom schemes. Check that the platform treats these as first-class. Provider gatekeeping: Google’s restricted scopes require a security assessment with annual reverification . Ask who owns that process, you or the platform, and what happens while verification is pending. 4. Reliability at scale An important part of reliability is not missing updates when data changes in third-party systems, which in practice means webhooks. Many providers tell you not to rely on webhooks alone: Stripe does not guarantee event ordering , and it retries failed deliveries for up to three days, and Shopify’s docs state that webhook delivery “isn’t always guaranteed” and recommend reconciliation jobs. Teams that had built replication on webhooks alone described silent data gaps that surfaced as customer incidents. What teams checked: Gap recovery: How does the platform detect and reconcile missed or out-of-order webhooks? Backfill limits: What are the execution time and memory limits, and what happens to a sync that exceeds them? Rate limits: Are provider limits handled per connection, and what happens when one customer’s burst consumes the quota? Tenant fairness: Does one large customer’s sync delay every other customer’s? 5. Observability you can debug with When an integration breaks, it usually breaks for one customer, on one connection, because of one payload. Teams wanted request-level logs per connection: what exactly was sent, what came back, and when. Teams that had used platforms without that visibility described the same loop: file a support ticket to debug your own product, wait, apologize to your customer, repeat. Several ranked the quality of error messages above the size of the catalog. What teams checked: Request-level logs: Every API call, per connection, with searchable payloads and sensitive fields redacted by default. A Management MCP server helps here, so coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) can debug failures directly from the logs. Error quality: Does a failure tell you which record failed and why, or does it say “sync failed”? Export: Can logs and traces flow into your existing monitoring stack (OpenTelemetry or similar), with your alerting rules? Audit trail: For enterprise buyers, a record of who changed what, and when. Log controls: Can you configure retention, access controls, data residency, and redaction so credentials and sensitive customer data do not leak into logs? 6. Deployment options and data residency For a large share of teams, deployment was a pass/fail filter applied before any feature discussion. EU customer data cannot flow through US-only infrastructure without a legal transfer pathway under GDPR Chapter V . Healthcare teams needed a business associate agreement signed before discussing features. Teams serving Singapore, the Gulf states, and regulated European industries brought residency requirements of their own. What teams checked: Regions: Where does the managed cloud run, and is there a region that satisfies your customers’ rules? Self-hosting: Is the self-hosted version at feature parity with the cloud, or a stripped-down build? Your own cloud: Can the platform run inside your AWS, GCP, or Azure account (BYOC), and who operates it there? Consistency: The same APIs and tooling across deployment modes, so you are not building twice. 7. Security posture An integration platform stores your customers’ credentials and executes API calls on their behalf. It becomes part of every security review and procurement process you go through. SOC 2 Type II reports and penetration tests came up on most calls. What teams checked: Who the end user authorizes: Does the OAuth consent screen show your app’s name or the platform’s? A third-party name on the consent screen raises questions in your customers’ security reviews. What an attacker gets: In May 2026, an attacker exfiltrated 5,001 GitHub OAuth tokens and 5,241 API keys from Composio . Teams asked how credentials are encrypted, how they are scoped, and what a compromise of the vendor’s own systems would expose. Shared OAuth apps: Shared developer apps are convenient. In production, a policy change or rate limit on a shared app affects every customer on it at once. Own your OAuth apps for anything that matters. 8. A pricing model you can project Integration platform pricing comes in many shapes: per connection, per task or record, by compute or concurrency, or a flat license. Per-connection pricing is expensive for products with many mostly idle connections. Per-task pricing is expensive for high-frequency syncs. Concurrency pricing is expensive for bursty workloads. What teams checked: Your shape at 10x: Model your own usage 12 to 18 months out, with your growth assumptions, and get the vendor to confirm the math. Inactive connections: Do you pay for connections nobody is using? The knobs: Can you tune sync frequency, switch polling to webhooks, or batch requests to control the bill yourself? Pass-through economics: If integrations are part of what you sell, does the model let you price them sanely for your own customers? 9. AI agent readiness Two separate questions hid under “does it work with AI agents”: Runtime, agents calling integrations: Products embedding AI agents need integrations exposed as tools: typed definitions the model can call, scoped per connection so an agent acting for one tenant cannot reach another tenant’s data. Teams building agent products asked for guardrails at the parameter level. Build time, agents building integrations: By mid-2026, “can our coding agent build the connector” had become a standard evaluation question. Teams wanted platforms that work well with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. What teams checked: Tenant isolation: Is every tool call bound to the correct customer connection on the server, rather than relying on the model to choose safely? Least privilege and approvals: Can you limit tools, scopes, and parameters per agent? Validated tool contracts: Are inputs and outputs typed and validated before an external API call runs? Production behavior: How does the platform handle retries, idempotency, timeouts, and audit logs when an agent repeats or partially completes an action? Build and release controls: Can coding agents test against real connections, submit generated source for review, and use the same versioning, CI, and rollback process as human-written integration code? 10. Exit path Vendors get acquired and roadmaps change: Workday announced its acquisition of Pipedream on November 19, 2025 . Teams that had been through a platform migration asked about the exit before they asked about the product. What teams checked: Credential portability: Can you export your customers’ tokens and API keys if you leave, or does leaving mean asking every customer to re-authorize? Data portability: Can you export synced data and configuration in a usable format? Source availability: Is the platform’s code public and auditable, and could you keep running it if the vendor disappeared? What teams did not ask about Vendor checklists emphasize three things that rarely came up on real evaluation calls: Unified data schemas: Teams building AI features told us normalized schemas matter less than they used to, because models handle raw API responses well. What they wanted was complete data, since fixed common schemas drop the custom fields they need. Visual workflow builders: Engineering teams treated low-code builders as a cost. They wanted integration logic in version control, code review, and CI like the rest of their product. Internal automation features: Teams distinguished sharply between product integrations (embedded in their app, used by their customers) and internal automation (connecting their own tools). iPaaS solutions built for internal workflows kept surfacing as mismatches for product use cases. How teams ran the evaluation The teams that made confident decisions ran the same shape of proof of concept, usually in one to two weeks: Pick your hardest integration, not your easiest: Any platform demos well on Slack. Evaluate it on NetSuite, SAP, or whatever the most complex item on your roadmap is. Test edge cases early: Add a custom field, call an endpoint the platform does not cover, and measure what that actually takes. Break things on purpose: Revoke a token mid-sync. Replay a webhook. Then read the logs and judge whether you could have debugged the failure without filing a support ticket. Start procurement in week one: Along with the technical evaluation, immediately send the compliance documents (SOC 2 report, DPA, BAA) to whoever runs security reviews. Model the bill at 10x: Get your projected usage priced before the trial ends. Where Nango fits Nango is an API integration platform with a catalog of 900+ APIs and enterprise-ready infrastructure built for scale and customization. Its code- and developer-first approach keeps integration logic under your control. Here is how Nango maps to the evaluation criteria above: Criterion Relevant Nango capabilities Control over integration logic TypeScript functions, editable source, CLI, Git and CI/CD, coding-agent workflows Catalog depth 900+ supported APIs, 6,000+ pre-built tools and syncs, flexibility to add your own provider or custom tools Complete auth handling Managed OAuth and API-key auth, token refresh, encrypted credential storage, branded Connect UI, pre-provisioned and customer-owned OAuth apps Reliability at scale Incremental syncs, webhooks, retries, pagination, rate-limit handling, connection-scoped execution Debuggable observability Per-connection logs, searchable requests, metrics and alerts, OpenTelemetry, Management MCP server (beta) Deployment and data residency Nango Cloud, enterprise self-hosting at feature parity with the cloud, BYOC on AWS, GCP, or Azure Security posture SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, HIPAA with a BAA, AES-256-GCM encryption, RBAC, SSO, scoped API keys, audit logs Projectable pricing Published unit pricing and included allowances for connections, proxy requests, compute, function runs, logs, sync storage, and webhooks. Volume discounts. AI agent readiness MCP and OpenAI-compatible tool definitions, connection-scoped actions, Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex support Exit path Open-source codebase, portable TypeScript source, self-hosting, credential export when using customer-owned OAuth apps Sources Coding-agent setup API integrations catalog Add or request an API provider Auth guide Observability Self-hosting Security Pricing Tool calling and MCP Nango GitHub repository If you are running an evaluation, use the quickstart to test these capabilities on one of your harder integrations. FAQ How do you choose an API integration platform? Choose based on how much control you keep over integration logic, whether the platform passes your customers’ security reviews, and whether the pricing model fits your usage shape at 10x scale. Then verify catalog depth against your specific roadmap with a one-to-two-week proof of concept on your hardest integration, and judge observability by debugging a failure you cause on purpose. What is the difference between an embedded iPaaS, a unified API, and an integration platform? An embedded iPaaS gives you low-code workflow tooling to build integrations one by one inside your product, a unified API gives you one normalized schema across a category of APIs, and broader integration platforms give you the infrastructure (auth, syncs, webhooks, observability) while integration logic stays under your control. Five ways to build product integrations in 2026 compares the approaches in depth. How do you manage multiple API integrations efficiently? Centralize what repeats across every integration (auth and token lifecycle, retries, rate limits, logging) in one layer, and keep per-API logic small, isolated, and in version control. Monitor per connection rather than per integration, because failures happen to individual customers. This is the main argument for using an API integration platform like Nango instead of accumulating one-off connectors. When does it make sense to build API integrations in-house? Building in-house makes sense when you have a small number of integrations, requirements too specific for any platform, and the capacity to own maintenance permanently, including provider breaking changes and token lifecycle infrastructure. Most of the cost shows up after the first version ships, in maintenance. Product integrations: build or buy? walks through the decision. What do AI agents change about evaluating integration platforms? Agents add two criteria: a runtime where agents call integrations as scoped, observable tools (MCP or OpenAI-compatible definitions), and build-time support for coding agents to create new integrations. The older criteria do not go away, because agents fail on the same auth, rate-limit, and reliability problems humans do.
